deck.hook: You bought 10 days to walk away. Most use four.

points.title: What The Fee Buys
body: The option fee is not a deposit on the house. It buys days.
Inside those days you can walk for any reason. Even a bad feeling in the driveway.
points.loop: You will not get all of them.

points.title: The Clock Started Yesterday
body: Day one is the day after both sides sign. Weekends count. Holidays count.
It dies at 5pm on the last day, not midnight.
points.loop: And that is before anyone shows up.

points.title: Where Six Days Go
body: A good inspector is booked three days out. The written report lands a day after that.
Ten days on paper. Four days to actually decide. That is the entire gap nobody warns you about.
points.loop: Deciding is not the same as done.

points.title: Silence Means You Bought It
body: Terminating is an action. Written notice, delivered, before the deadline hour.
Nobody calls to remind you. The contract just quietly hardens around you.
points.loop: Walking is rarely what you want.

points.title: Repairs Are A Race
body: Any price cut or repair promise has to be signed inside that same window. Not after it.
A seller who stalls until 4:55 knows exactly what they are doing.
points.loop: This gets solved before you offer.

linkedinCaption:
The Texas option period is the most misunderstood part of a residential contract, and the confusion is usually about time, not money.

The fee does not go toward the house. It buys days. Day one is the day after execution. Weekends and holidays count. It ends at 5pm, not midnight.

A ten day option period is rarely ten days of decision making. Inspectors book out. Reports take a day to write. What is left is often four days to read, price out repairs, and negotiate.

Termination requires written notice delivered before the deadline. Silence is a purchase.

For the agents here: what length option period are you seeing hold up best in your market right now?
